clue.text: Produce most favourable result, but stated grade description's wrong!

indicators.note: something stated is spoken, so the solver listens to the description rather than reading it

parts.note: a mistaken description of the B grade, since A is really the top mark

explanation.surface: Someone is grumbling that a school report has the grades muddled.
explanation.walkthrough: Saying 'B for the best' would be wrong, because A is the best grade; spoken aloud it is the phrase BE FOR THE BEST.
explanation.definitionFit: If something will be for the best, it turns out with the happiest outcome available.

clue.text: Puffed out, having rowed across lake

indicators.note: having gone across something means lying on either side of it, so one piece wraps round the other

parts.note: went by boat
L is the map abbreviation for lake

explanation.surface: A rower is left breathless and swollen after crossing a lake.
explanation.definitionFit: Bloated describes something swollen or distended, as by gas or overindulgence.

clue.text: Dingy hole has made one dreadfully pale — well out of it!

indicators.note: one piece stands outside the other, which sits within it

parts.note: healthy, in good shape

indicators.note: something done dreadfully is done badly, so these letters come out jumbled

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A grim little den has left a visitor looking ill, and they are glad to be out of it.
explanation.walkthrough: A FLEAPIT is British slang for a shabby, run-down cinema or theatre.
explanation.definitionFit: A fleapit is a shabby, squalid place of entertainment, supposedly infested with vermin.

clue.text: One's shot — and shoot in quick succession

parts.note: a stretch of fast water that a canoeist shoots
to discharge a gun

explanation.surface: Gunfire talk: someone fires, then fires again straight away.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Shot' is past tense of shooting the rapids: a rapid is one thing that is shot.
explanation.definitionFit: Rapid-fire describes questions or shots delivered one after another without pause.

clue.text: Explosive level produced from sulphur

parts.note: HE is the abbreviation for high explosive
on a par means at the same level

explanation.surface: A chemistry note about an explosive compound being made from sulphur.
explanation.walkthrough: HEPAR is an old chemistry term: 'liver of sulphur', a compound made by fusing sulphur with potash.
explanation.definitionFit: Hepar is the alchemists' name for liver-coloured substances made by heating sulphur with alkali.

clue.text: Demolished loaf of bread in style

indicators.note: to style something is to fashion it into a new shape, so these letters are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A baker's loaf is smashed, styled to look like fancy bread.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Loaf' is slang for the head, so a demolished loaf is a head that has been struck hard.
explanation.definitionFit: To brain someone is to hit them violently on the head, so a smashed head has been brained.

clue.text: Turn love letters, first and last, over to writer

parts.note: a rotation
zero in tennis scoring

indicators.note: turned over means flipped end to end, so the alphabet's ends are read in the opposite order

parts.note: the first and last letters of the alphabet

explanation.surface: Someone flips over a love letter, start and finish, before handing it to an author.
explanation.walkthrough: Baruch Spinoza was the 17th-century Dutch philosopher, writer of the Ethics.
explanation.definitionFit: Spinoza is a famous philosophical author, so he serves as an example of a writer.

clue.text: Furnishes houses

definitions.meaning: first meaning: supplies or provides with something
second meaning: provides lodging for, a verb

explanation.walkthrough: 'Houses' reads as a plural noun next to 'Furnishes', but it is a verb like the other.
explanation.definitionFit: To accommodate is both to supply someone with what they need and to give them a place to stay.

clue.text: Come together for photo

definitions.meaning: first meaning: to draw tight, closing gaps between people
second meaning: a picture taken at very short range

explanation.surface: A photographer asks a group to bunch up for the picture.
explanation.definitionFit: Ranks close up when they move nearer each other; a close-up is a tightly framed photograph.

clue.text: Map is hard to roll

parts.note: a plan is a drawn map of a site
taken as written
H is the pencil abbreviation for hard

explanation.surface: A map is stiff and difficult to roll up.
explanation.definitionFit: Planishing flattens sheet metal by hammering or passing it through polished rollers.

clue.text: Grandsire to exchange, following hard bargaining

indicators.note: coming after means the rearranged letters sit behind the single letter

parts.note: H is the pencil abbreviation for hard

indicators.note: items in an exchange swap places, so these letters trade positions

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A grandfather is to be swapped after some tough haggling.
explanation.definitionFit: Horse-trading is shrewd, hard-nosed negotiation, named after the haggling of horse dealers.

clue.text: Having no fish, consumed prime sort of mollusc

parts.note: O looks like a zero, nothing

indicators.note: what is consumed ends up inside the eater, so one piece swallows the other

parts.note: a common food fish
first-rate, the best

explanation.surface: Someone without fish to eat makes do with a top-quality shellfish.
explanation.definitionFit: Octopods are the eight-armed cephalopods, a class of molluscs that includes the octopus.

clue.text: Expressed private resentment

indicators.note: something expressed is put into words and spoken, so the sound matters rather than spelling

parts.note: a private soldier is a ranker, serving in the ranks

explanation.surface: Someone voices bitterness they had kept to themselves.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Private' looks like an adjective meaning secret; it is the soldier. The two words sound alike in a British accent that drops the final r.
explanation.definitionFit: Rancour is deep, long-held bitterness and ill will, a close synonym.

clue.text: Halfwits — stupid, backward and in the thick of things

definitions.note: MIDST used as a poetic preposition, meaning amid

indicators.note: backward means the combined string is read from its end to its start
only half of the word survives, so its front pair of letters goes

parts.note: the word wits, of which only the second half is kept
slow-witted

explanation.surface: Idiots, dim and slow, find themselves at the centre of the action.
explanation.definitionFit: Midst, as in 'midst the throng', is an old poetic form of amid, among or surrounded by.

clue.text: Urgent item broadcast across all news channels

indicators.note: lying across something means spanning it on both sides, so one piece encloses the other
broadcast means scattered widely, so these letters are strewn into a new order

parts.note: taken as written
the media is the collective term for news outlets

explanation.surface: A breaking story is being aired on every news network at once.
explanation.definitionFit: An immediate matter needs attention at once, which is what an urgent one demands.

clue.text: He may wickedly leave you without a leg to stand on

definitions.text: He may wickedly leave you without a leg to stand on

parts.words: He may wickedly leave you without a leg to stand on
parts.note: surface reading: someone who cruelly destroys your argument

parts.words: without a leg to stand on
parts.note: setter's reading: literally, someone who has cut off a limb

explanation.walkthrough: The idiom for losing an argument is taken literally: a person who chops off your leg.
explanation.definitionFit: A mutilator is someone who maims a body by cutting off or damaging limbs.

clue.text: The man's tucked in — fit to burst!

definitions.note: the answer is an adjective, ready to burst open

indicators.note: something tucked in is pushed inside, so one piece sits within another

parts.note: fit to be seen, respectable
belonging to him

explanation.surface: A man who has eaten his fill feels fit to burst.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fit' sits beside 'to burst' as one phrase but serves as the outer piece.
explanation.definitionFit: Botanists call a seed pod dehiscent when it splits open naturally to release its contents.

clue.text: Nurse seeking asylum

definitions.meaning: first meaning: to keep a feeling in mind, as with a grudge
second meaning: a place of shelter or refuge

explanation.surface: A nurse is looking for refuge, or a job at a mental hospital.
explanation.definitionFit: One harbours or nurses a grudge, and a harbour is a refuge or safe haven.

clue.text: Sing, disregarding a companion wanting silence

indicators.note: what is disregarded is left out, so the following small word is dropped

parts.note: underworld slang: to inform on someone
taken as written, the letter to drop
CH is a Companion of Honour

explanation.surface: A singer, ignoring their partner, longs for quiet.
explanation.walkthrough: To sing and to squeal both mean to inform to the police. The Companion of Honour is a British order whose holders put CH after their names.
explanation.definitionFit: To squelch someone is to crush or silence them, as with a sharp put-down.

clue.text: Vestment right for one 10

parts.note: a long cloak worn by clergy
R is the abbreviation for right

explanation.surface: A priest's robe is right for someone in the trade.
explanation.walkthrough: The 10 refers to 10-down, horse-trading; a coper is an old word for a horse dealer.
explanation.definitionFit: A coper is a dealer in horses, so one engaged in horse-trading.

clue.text: Did lag do time previously in this connection?

indicators.note: coming previously means placed earlier, so the time unit goes ahead of the verb

parts.note: a lag is a convict, and to do someone is to con them
T is the abbreviation for time
perform

explanation.surface: Someone asks whether an old prisoner served a sentence earlier in the matter under discussion.
explanation.walkthrough: A lag is British slang for a habitual criminal or convict.
explanation.definitionFit: Contact means a link or touch between people or things, so it is a connection.

clue.text: He may play the game and break the law

definitions.meaning: first meaning: a doubles player who takes shots meant for a partner
second meaning: one who illegally hunts game on another's land

explanation.walkthrough: 'Play the game' sounds like behaving fairly, which jars with lawbreaking; the game is also the birds and deer that are taken illegally.
explanation.definitionFit: In tennis a player who poaches intercepts a partner's shot; a lawbreaking hunter steals game.

clue.text: High rock reportedly of importance to this resort

parts.note: a rocky hill, common on Dartmoor

indicators.note: a report is what someone says, so the meaning is heard rather than spelt

parts.note: crucial, vital

explanation.surface: A tall crag is said to matter a great deal to a seaside town.
explanation.walkthrough: TORQUAY is a seaside resort in Devon, in south-west England, near Dartmoor's tors.
explanation.definitionFit: Torquay is a well-known English holiday town on the coast of Devon, so it is a resort.

clue.text: Battle of, say, Prestonpans

indicators.note: letters made of the following words are taken from within them

parts.note: the run of letters spanning the two words

explanation.surface: A query asks about the Battle of Prestonpans, an example given.
explanation.walkthrough: Prestonpans was a 1745 Jacobite battle in Scotland; the answer is the Belgian town of three First World War battles.
explanation.definitionFit: Ypres in Flanders gave its name to several major battles of the First World War.

clue.text: Retrieve from water fish pulled back in with line

indicators.note: one piece goes inside the other

parts.note: to haul a catch ashore

indicators.note: pulling something back draws it the other way, so the creature's name runs right to left

parts.note: a flat sea fish

explanation.surface: An angler reels a catch from the water on the end of a line.
explanation.definitionFit: A lanyard is a short cord or rope, used on ships to secure things or worn round the neck.

clue.text: One to frown, that is, to lower if put differently

parts.note: SC is short for scilicet, Latin for namely or that is

indicators.note: putting a word differently means arranging its letters another way

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A definition of a frowner as someone who glowers, phrased another way.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Lower' here also means to frown, rhyming with 'glower', which makes the surface read like a dictionary entry.
explanation.definitionFit: A scowler is a person with an angry, frowning expression on their face.

clue.text: Drink and endless crack following lecture

indicators.note: with no end, the final letter of the word is cut off

parts.note: a hot drink
a narrow gap or opening

explanation.surface: After a talk, people have a cuppa and a bit of banter.
explanation.definitionFit: A teach-in is an extended informal lecture or discussion session, popular on campuses in the 1960s.

clue.text: Or that scorer, perhaps?

indicators.note: perhaps hints the words could be otherwise, so their letters may be rearranged

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone wonders whether a sports scorer, or some such person, is meant.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue is the definition: a scorer arranges music for an orchestra, and the letters of the first three words rearrange to the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: A scorer writes out music for instruments, which is just what an arranger for an orchestra does.
